stem:
A 29-year-old with bipolar I disorder is well on valproate after several previous manic admissions. She uses reliable contraception, has a negative pregnancy test and plans to try to conceive in three months. At a GP appointment she asks whether she should stop both valproate and contraception today. Her psychiatrist can review her within a week.

What is the best advice now?

options.label: A
options.text: Stop valproate today and continue contraception until the review
options.explanation: The treatment must be reviewed before conception, but abrupt unsupervised cessation can destabilise her bipolar disorder. A prompt planned change is safer than stopping on her own.

options.label: B
options.text: Stop contraception and continue valproate with folic acid
options.explanation: Folic acid does not remove valproate’s fetal risks. Contraception should not be stopped while this treatment plan is being resolved.

options.label: C
options.text: Maintain contraception pending a specialist medication change
options.explanation: She needs prompt specialist planning to replace or discontinue valproate before conception and before stopping contraception. Until that plan is agreed, she should not abruptly stop medication herself.

options.label: D
options.text: Continue the current regimen until pregnancy is confirmed
options.explanation: Waiting for pregnancy misses the opportunity to avoid early fetal exposure. Pregnancy planning is the time to change the treatment strategy.

options.label: E
options.text: Reduce valproate herself before stopping contraception
options.explanation: An unsupervised reduction does not establish a safe preconception regimen or remove fetal risk. The change should be planned with her specialist.

context: For bipolar disorder, plan a specialist-supervised transition away from valproate before conception; maintain contraception while the plan is implemented.
